title: Ang 1232–1236: Sarang ashtpadis
tomorrow: a ballad in the middle of Sarang? whose story does it sing?
last: THE NINTH: WHOSE MOTHER, WHOSE FATHER?

lines: A TEXT, OR AN ELEVEN-MINUTE MEMO.
cards: Some things fit in a text. Some need a voice memo that runs eleven minutes, where you keep circling back to the one thing you actually called to say. On ang 1232, Sarang changes its heading to asatpadeeaa: longer hymns.
Same raga, same Gurus, more stanzas. So why would a Guru need the longer form?

teach.b: Because some things need walking around. A short hymn says it and stops. A longer one takes one longing and turns it, stanza by stanza, like walking all the way around a tree to see it whole.
And it doesn't get lost, because it still has a rahau, the pause line, the center every stanza leans back toward.
Something to tell a friend tonight: in kirtan, the singers return to the rahau between stanzas, so even a listener who loses the thread gets handed the center again.

teach.h: HOW CAN I LIVE WITHOUT YOU?
teach.b: One of these Sarang hymns, in paraphrase, opens: without the Lord, how can I live, my mother? Then it spends its length on that one question.

That's the two weeks behind us, too, if you walk around them: nothing outside the One; one clay; serve the One; the Name not knotted; the milk; what's seen will pass; forever spring; Ramanand, colored at home; the Name running cool at noon.

how: Readers find the longer hymns under the heading asatpadeeaa after the shorter hymns in a raga; in kirtan, ragis return to the rahau line between stanzas, and the sangat can sing it with them.

games.q: you're giving a short goodbye speech at a friend's going-away party. you have one thing you really want to say, and a few stories. how does a longer hymn suggest you build it?

games.why: a longer hymn turns one longing stanza by stanza and keeps returning to its rahau, so it can be long without getting lost.

practice: Take a scrap of paper and write, by hand, the one line from these two weeks you'd want to keep. Just one. Then sit with it in front of you, your rahau, and let the other lines circle it.
If you'd like, read ang 1232 before you begin.
